description: Henry Schein is a global health care services distributor of dental and medical supplies, business and supply-chain solutions, and tech-forward integrated care solutions. The nearly century-old company operates in over 30 countries and has developed more than 300,000 products, from diagnostics to surgical and orthopedics, including whitening strips, dental implants, patient communication services, and a dual-cuff blood pressure monitor. In early 2025 the company acquired Acentus, a national medical supplier of continuous glucose monitors, to expand its portfolio. Henry Schein has been named among the World’s Most Ethical Companies by Ethisphere for 13 consecutive years.

title: Henry Schein

rankings.title: Change the World
rankings.itemDescription: Health care product distributor Henry Schein has redoubled its effort to provide in-kind donations and grants to disaster-stricken areas, as well as to work with NGOs to proactively supply vulnerable areas with medical and dental supplies—so supplies are there even if roads or airports become unusable. Its Global Product Donation Program has donated over $75 million in health care supplies to health centers and clinics since its 1998 inception. Henry Schein also provides $10,000 in cash grants and $25,000 in products through its Prepare to Care Program to each of five nonprofit partners committed to disaster-relief preparedness and immediate assistance in natural disaster-prone areas.

rankings.title: Change the World
rankings.itemDescription: As with many aspects of daily living, the standard dentist visit was not designed with much consideration for the needs of those with disabilities. For some, the experience may be physically inaccessible; for others, like those with developmental disabilities such as autism, the environment and experience—with its bright lights, buzzing noises, and close contact—can be terrifying and traumatic. Meanwhile, in part due to those challenges, people with disabilities suffer higher rates and more severe cases of periodontal disease, gum disease, and untreated cavities—all conditions that can lead to other health problems. Henry Schein, the dental and medical supply company, began work to address this disparity more than a decade ago, forging partnerships—like Project Accessible Oral Health—to increase training and adapt dental practices to better serve disabled people. The efforts have resulted in provision of specialized services to hundreds of thousands of children as well as a new dental school curriculum, developed with stakeholders like the American Dental Education Association.

rankings.title: Fortune 500
rankings.itemDescription: Founded by its namesake as a Queens, N.Y., pharmacy in 1932, the company is now one of the world's largest distributors of dental supplies and other medical goods, operating in more than 30 countries. An ever-present on Fortune's list of the World's Most Admired Companies, it is considered by many in its sector as a leader in social responsibility. With $10.1 billion in sales last year, Henry Schein moved up six spots on this year's Fortune 500 list.

rankings.title: Fortune 500
rankings.itemDescription: Long Island's largest public company by revenue, Melville, N.Y.-based Henry Schein globally distributes medical and dental supplies including vaccines, pharmaceuticals, financial services, and equipment. The company kicked off 2019 by spinning out its animal health unit in an attempt to focus on its core medical and dental businesses; it ended the year with the novel coronavirus pandemic eroding its business.

rankings.title: Change the World
rankings.itemDescription:
Five years ago, well before COVID-19 entered the lexicon, Henry Schein CEO Stan Bergman called on his peers at the World Economic Forum to think collectively about pandemic preparedness. It worried him that there was no organized emergency product list, and no directory of where to get such products when emergency struck. Soon after, Bergman’s dental and medical supply company became a founder and the private-sector lead of the Pandemic Supply Chain Network, a public-private partnership whose members include the World Health Organization, the World Bank, UPS, and more than five dozen health care manufacturers.

The group created a platform to convene responders and exchange information. Says Bergman: “You can’t do it in the middle of a pandemic. You’ve got to exchange business cards well before.” The network functioned well in recent Ebola outbreaks, and in response to COVID-19, it has sourced more than $200 million worth of critical supplies, like masks, gowns, and swabs, so far.
